d: Speech you make to yourself
ety: 1595–1605; From Late Latin sōliloquium in the title of St. Augustine's Soliloquiorum libri duo ("Two Books of Soliloquies"), from sōlus (“only, sole”) + loquor (“to speak”).
s: At the end of the second act the main villain gave a soliloquy detailing his plans to attack the protagonist.

d: A structure or device in which one end is counterbalanced by the other (on the principle of the seesaw)
ety: From French bascule, from earlier French bacule, from Old French bacul, from Old French battre + cul, from Latin battuō (“beat”) + cul (“bottom”).
s: A device for coupling and releasing the trigger mechanism in a bascule of a gun

d: Personal state of isolation and anxiety resulting from a lack of social control and regulation
ety: From French anomie, from Ancient Greek ἀνομία (anomía, “lawlessness”), from ἄνομος (ánomos, “lawless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). Popularized by French sociologist Émile Durkheim (1858–1917).
s: No wonder, then, that all of these women are consigned to their lot. What’s the point? From adolescent traumas to adulthood indignities, their anomie has been overdetermined.

d: A wooden hand tool with a pointed end; used to make holes in the ground for planting seeds or bulbs
ety: Possibly dib (“to dab lightly”) + -le (frequentative suffix indicating repetition or continuousness); however, the word dibble is attested earlier than dib.
s: Watch out, lads! Here comes the dibble!

d: Painful grief
ety: From Middle English dolour (“physical pain, agony, suffering; painful disease; anguish, grief, misery, sorrow; grieving for sins, contrition; hardship, misery, trouble; cause of grief or suffering, affliction”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman dolour, Old French dolour, dolor, dulur (“pain”) (modern French douleur (“pain; distress”)), from Latin dolor (“ache, hurt, pain; anguish, grief, sorrow
s: Perchance a congregation to fulfil / Solemnities of silence in this doom, / Mysterious rites of dolour and despair / Permitting not a breath or chant of prayer?

d: Hypothetical remedy for all ills or diseases; once sought by the alchemists
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin nostrum (“ours”), nominative neuter of noster (“our, ours”).
s: After each day's work in the fields, Brown was given some nostrum and made to repeat the ordeal.

d: A window with glass louvers
ety: Borrowed from French jalousie. Doublet of jealousy.
s: Nowhere the glitter of a glass casement; Venetian blinds, jalousies, closed every window, and rooms projected in all directions to catch the luxury of a through-draft of air.

d: Walk or tramp about
ety: Likely from French trépasser (“pass over or beyond”).
s: After traipsing about in the fog they found the grave sure enough.

d: Someone employed in a stable to take care of the horses
ety: Phonetic spelling of hostler, from late 14th century.
s: Followed by the sun, I left the grounds of the mansion and entered the deserted park, an ostler leading a large and passive work-horse out to the day's labour.

d: A relaxed comfortable feeling
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English langore, langour (“disease, illness; misery, sadness; suffering; condition or event causing sadness, suffering, etc.; unwholesomeness; idleness, inertia; depression, self-disgust; expression of grief”) [and other forms], from Middle French languer, langueur, langour, and Anglo-Norman langor, langour, langur, Old French langueur, languour (“disease, illness;
s: Sometimes my pulse beat so quickly and hardly, that I felt the palpitation of every artery; at others, I nearly sank to the ground through languor and extreme weakness.

d: Catch sight of
ety: From Middle English descrien, descriven in the 14th century already had the dual sense of "to proclaim, announce, make known" and "to see, discern, discover". On the one hand, the Middle English word is a loan Old French descrier (“to proclaim, announce, cry”), from des- + crier (“shout, cry”); in this case, the word is a doublet of decry, which was loaned from the same French source in the 17th c
s: Wee haue descryed vpon our neighbouring / shore, a portlie saile of ships make hitherward.

d: A frame made of two hoops; used for embroidering
ety: Borrowed from French tambour (“drum”), from Arabic طُنْبُور (ṭunbūr), from the Middle Persian ancestor of Classical Persian تنبور (tanbūr). Doublet of tabor and tanbur. Compare Armenian տաւիղ (tawiġ), and tabla.
s: Recollect Lady Teazle when I saw you first—sitting at your tambour in a pretty figured linen gown—

d: Cause oneself to consider something
ety: From Middle English bethenken, bithenchen (“to think about, consider”) from Old English beþenċan, biþenċan (“to think upon, remind, consider, remember”), from Proto-Germanic *biþankijaną; equivalent to be- + think. Akin to Old High German pidenchan (German bedenken), Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐌸𐌰𐌲𐌺𐌾𐌰𐌽 (biþagkjan), Dutch bedenken.
s: He showed the two men from Vinland how to fit the rubber masks over their noses. “Bethink you to outbreathe through your mouths, and you’ll be fine.”

d: So thin as to transmit light
ety: From Medieval Latin diaphanus, from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs), from δια- (dia-, “through”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).
s: Adam requires a touch of feminine lace and a whisper of diaphanous silk, not a direct vision of the gaping maw of the human vulva.

d: A feeling of deep regret (usually for some misdeed)
ety: From Middle English compunccion, borrowed from Old French compunction, from Late Latin compunctionem (“a pricking”), from Latin compunctus, the past participle of compungere (“to severely prick”), from com- + pungere (“to prick”).
s: As for average U.S. consumers, they've shown little compunction about buying diamonds that fund bloody militias in Africa.

d: A sudden uncontrollable attack
ety: From Late Middle English paroxism, paroxisme (“period of worsening of a disease, attack; sudden recurrent fever”), from Middle French paroxisme, paroxysme, and Old French peroxime (“period of worsening of a disease; bout of fever or illness”) (modern French paroxysme), and from their etymon Late Latin paroxismus, paroxysmus (“a fit; onset of a disease; violent impulse or sadness”), from Ancient Gr
s: The slightest effort made the patient cough. He would stand leaning on a stick and holding a hand to his side, and when the paroxysm had passed it left him shaking.

d: Dwelling beneath the surface of the earth
ety: From Ancient Greek χθόνιος (khthónios, “in or under the ground”), from χθών (khthṓn, “ground”).
s: The Olympian religion is truly Olympian when it rests on Chthonian grounds, and the Chthonian religion is truly Chthonian when it stands in the Olympian light.

d: A confused multitude of things
ety: From Middle English welteren, equivalent to welt + -er (frequentative suffix). Cognates include German Low German weltern (“to wallow; roll”), Old Norse velta (Danish vælte), German wälzen, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌻𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (waltjan). Akin to wallow and Latin volvō.
s: They use these words to express a welter of opinions on what they think is good or bad, right or wrong, and all too readily wail ‘It's not fair!’.

d: A sandal with a sole made of rope or rubber and a cloth upper part
ety: Borrowed from French espadrille.
s: She wore loose black silks and black espadrilles.

d: A violent hot sand-laden wind on the deserts of Arabia and North Africa
ety: From Arabic سَمُوم (samūm, “hot wind”), from سَمَّ (samma, “to poison”).
s: Stephen's heart had withered up like a flower of the desert that feels the simoom coming from afar.

d: Suitable for the general public
ety: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Late Latin exōtericus + English -ic (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). Exōtericus is borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξωτερῐκός (exōterĭkós, “exterior, external, outside”, adjective), from ἐξωτέρω (exōtérō, “more exterior”) (the comparative form of ἔξω (éxō, “external, outer”) (ultimately from ἐκ (ek, “beyond; outside”, prepositi
s: Writings of an exoteric nature.

d: Free from slavery or servitude
ety: From Middle English manumitten, from Latin manūmittere, from pre-Classical Latin manū ēmittere (literally “send out from one’s hand”).
s: Ruth wept much but Sara set her beauty to a fierce grimness which, even when, as you shall hear later, she was manumitted, she never entirely lost.

d: A stubborn person of arbitrary or arrogant opinions
ety: Borrowed from French doctrinaire, from doctrine + -aire.
s: Or, shall we play the doctrinaire, and hint that at thirty-four the tides of life are calmer and cognizant of many sources instead of but one—as at four-and-twenty?

d: Having no cause or apparent cause
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin fortuītus (“happening by chance, accidental, random, fortuitous”), from *fortu- (“chance, fortune, luck”) + -ītus (suffix forming adjectives). *Fortu- is thought to be from *fortus, from fors (“chance, luck”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”)) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns). Doublet of fortuity.
s: Was it love, she wondered, or a mere fortuitous combination of happy thoughts and sensations?

d: Anger produced by some annoying irritation
ety: From Late Middle English vexacioun, vexation (“physical suffering; act of inflicting trouble (specifically through unjustified legal action); anxiety, mental distress; mental disturbance”), from Anglo-Norman vexacion, vexation, Middle French vexacion, vexation (“distress, suffering; harassment (specifically through unjustified legal action)”), and Old French vexacion, vexation (“distress, sufferin
s: He clenched his fists in vexation and looked up at her impetuously.

d: Not tractable; difficult to manage or mold
ety: From in- + tractable.
s: Work—bureaucratic work in particular—poses a series of intractable dilemmas that often demand compromises with traditional moral beliefs.

d: Make off with belongings of others
ety: From Middle English purloynen (“to remove”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman purloigner (“to put far away”), one of the variants of Old French porloignier. Doublet of prolong.
s: Had from his wakeful custody purloined / The guarded gold.

d: In an advanced stage of pregnancy
ety: From Latin gravidus (“laden, pregnant”), from gravis (“heavy”).
s: One slender hand was raised in a graceful gesture gravid with meaning.

d: A container where religious relics are stored or displayed (especially relics of saints)
ety: Borrowed from Middle French reliquaire (modern French reliquaire), from Late Latin reliquiarium, from rēliquia (“a relic”) (English relic), noun use of reliquus (“abandoned, left behind, relict”), from relinquō (“to relinquish”), from re- (“again”) and linquō (“to leave”), from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-.
s: And whether you think of those little cans as intellectual puzzles or reliquaries or scams, there are surprises inside.

d: Perceiving the significance of events before they occur
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin praesciēns (“foreknowing; foretelling, predicting”), present participle of) Latin praesciō (“to foreknow”), from prae- (prefix meaning ‘before; in front’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before; in front”)) + sciō (“to know, understand; to have knowledge of”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to dissect; to split”)). The word is cognate with
s: Members opposite seem to be prescient; they seem to know what I am going to say before I have said it.

d: Large metal container in which coal or charcoal is burned; warms people who must stay outside for long times
ety: From Middle English brasiere, from brasen (“to cover with brass”), from Old English brasian, bræsian (“to cover with brass”). By surface analysis, bras(s) + -ier.
s: One of them came forward, and, producing a lamp, lit it from his brazier (for the Amahagger when on a journey nearly always carried with them a little lighted brazier, from which to provide fire).

d: An assistant to a bishop
ety: From Middle English coadjutowre, from Old French coadjuteur, borrowed from Late Latin coadiūtōrem, from co- + adiūtor (“helper”), from adiuvō (“to help”) + -tor (agent suffix). By surface analysis, co- + adjutor. The French derivation gave the accentuation co⁠ˈadjutor (used by Samuel Taylor Coleridge), but the poets generally, since 1600, appear to have coa⁠ˈdjutor, after Latin. No Latin *coadiuvō
s: August then appointed Prince George III of Anhalt (who was both a theologian and a priest as well as a prince) to be his coadjutor in spiritual matters.

d: Return or recoil
ety: From Anglo-Norman redunder, Middle French redonder, and their source, Latin redundō, from red- + undō (“surge”), from unda (“a wave”).
s: His infamous behaviour only redounded back upon him when he was caught.

d: Teaching pupils individually (usually by a tutor hired privately)
ety: From Latin tūtēla (“a watching, guardianship, protection”) + -age, from tuērī (“to watch, guard”). See tuition.
s: But when asked which of his achievements he is most proud of, he says: “Actually those of others hypermilers behind the wheel, thanks to my tutelage or simply inspiration.”

d: Serving to bring to mind
ety: From Middle English redolent (first attested in 1400), from Old French redolent, from Latin redolentem, present participle of redoleō (“to emit a scent”), from red- + oleō (“to smell”).
s: His breath is already redolent of whiskey.

d: Have or develop complicating consequences
ety: Borrowed from Middle French ramifier, from Medieval Latin ramificō (“to branch, ramify”), from Latin rāmus (“a branch”) + -ficō (causative suffix).
s: The cortical, hemispheral or superficial veins ramify on the surface of the brain and return the blood from the cortical substance into the venous sinuses.

d: Preoccupation with the acquisition and possession of books
ety: From biblio- + -mania.
s: To collect books indiscriminately tends to develop the dread bibliomania.

d: Marked by blithe unconcern
ety: From French insouciant, from in- (“not”, prefix) + souciant (“worrying”), 1828.
s: An utterly insouciant financial policy.

d: The bodily property of being well rounded
ety: Borrowed from French embonpoint.
s: She was slightly inclined to embonpoint.

d: Conducive to peace
ety: From Ancient Greek εἰρηνικός (eirēnikós, “characterized by peace, peaceful”) + English -ic (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). Εἰρηνικός (Eirēnikós) is derived from εἰρήνη (eirḗnē, “peace”) (possibly from εἴρω (eírō, “to fasten together”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“(verb) to bind, tie together; (noun) thread”)), or εἴρω (eírō, “to say, speak”) (ultim
s: The idea that the Jews of the region are not genetically distinct from other peoples of the area should be an irenic insight.
